contentBlocks.text: This week you've learned structure, audience adaptation, and combined appeals. Today: analyze one complete passage using everything!

Read this complete short speech excerpt, aimed at a school board considering funding for a new community garden program: 'I've spent five years volunteering at gardens across this district, and I've seen the numbers: participating families cut their grocery bills by nearly a third. But numbers only tell part of the story. I've watched a shy new student find her first real friend group over a row of tomato plants — a connection no budget line item can capture. This board has the chance to fund something that pays for itself twice: once in dollars, and once in the kind of belonging every student deserves.' Write a short paragraph analyzing this complete passage: identify its audience adaptation, its rhetorical structure, and how its appeals work together.
You just wrote a complete advanced rhetorical analysis! Tomorrow we'll review everything from this week.

objectives: Combine structure, audience-adaptation, and combined-appeals analysis into one written paragraph
Write a coherent complete analysis of the school-board speech excerpt
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's structure, audience-adaptation, and combined-appeals work together.
2. Read the complete speech excerpt together.
3. Have the child write their full analysis paragraph.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's cumulative review.
differentiationTips: Struggling: have the child answer three separate guiding questions (Who's the audience, and how is it adapted? What's the structure/climax? Where are the appeals?) before combining them into one paragraph
Ready for more: ask the child to identify the single most persuasive sentence in the passage, and explain exactly why it works so well
This is the week's synthesis moment — combining all three advanced rhetorical-analysis skills into one coherent written analysis is the genuinely important skill here
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is an open-ended analysis activity — check that the paragraph identifies the school-board audience adaptation (emphasizing both cost savings AND belonging, since a school board cares about both budget and student wellbeing), the climax structure (saving the emotional 'belonging' point for last), and how ethos (five years volunteering), logos (a third off grocery bills), and pathos (the shy student finding friendship) reinforce each other throughout.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Grade 11-12 RI.11-12.6 in full, synthesizing this week's three advanced rhetorical-analysis skills before tomorrow's review.
